**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference to Its Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Typical Value / Description |
|----------|----------|-----------------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | State at STP | Gas (colorless, odorless, tasteless) |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (−423.2 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (−434.6 °F) |
| | Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | 0.754 eV |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Second ionization energy | 27.211 eV |
| | Heat of formation (gas) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation (liquid) | –285.83 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Standard entropy (gas) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat capacity (gas, 25 °C) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound in H₂ | ~1270 m s⁻¹ (at 20 °C) |
| | Refractive index (visible) | ~1.000132 |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.792847 µB (for proton) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 1 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| **Chemical Behavior** | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (H₂) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Acidic character | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) |
| | Basic character | Forms hydrides (e.g., NaH, CaH₂) |
| | Redox behavior | Strong reducing agent (e.g., in metal hydrides) |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Bond length (H–H) | 0.74 Å |
| | Dipole moment (H₂) | 0 (homonuclear diatomic) |
| | Polarity of H‑containing molecules | Depends on partner atoms (e.g., H₂O is polar) |
| **Physical & Thermodynamic** | Vapor pressure (at 25 °C) | ~1.3 kPa |
| | Critical temperature | 33.0 K |
| | Critical pressure | 1.3 MPa |
| | Critical density | 0.07 g cm⁻³ |
| | Compressibility factor (Z) | Near 1 at low pressures |
| | Specific heat ratio (γ) | 1.41 (ideal diatomic gas) |
| | Thermal conductivity (gas) | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 25 °C) |
| | Viscosity (gas) | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa s (at 25 °C) |
| **Spectroscopic** | Rotational spectrum | Microwave region (e.g., 2.1 cm⁻¹ for H₂) |
| | Vibrational frequency (H₂) | 4401 cm⁻¹ |
| | Electronic transitions | UV–visible absorption (e.g., 121.6 nm Lyman‑α line) |
| | Isotopic shifts | Deuterium shows ~2× lower vibrational frequency |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant (~99.98 %) |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, ~0.02 % natural abundance |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion & radiolabeling |
| | Deuterium‑tritium mixture | Fuel for D‑T fusion (neutron yield) |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel cell (PEM) | H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, electricity |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for metal extraction |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydride source, hydrogenation reactions |
| | Medical imaging | ¹H MRI (proton imaging) |
| | Nuclear fusion | D‑T fusion, magnetic confinement experiments |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage (compressed, liquid, metal hydrides) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; wide flammability range (4–75 % H₂ in air) |
| | Explosion risk | High pressure + spark → explosion |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but can cause hypoxia by displacing oxygen |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders, cryogenic tanks, or metal hydride beds |
| | Environmental impact | Low CO₂ emissions when used as fuel; production may involve fossil fuels |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) one neutron (protium).
- **It exists mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but also as ions (H⁺, H⁻) and in various compounds.
- **Its isotopes** (deuterium, tritium) are crucial for nuclear fusion research and isotope labeling in chemistry.
- **Physically**, it is the lightest, most abundant element in the universe, with a very low boiling point and high speed of sound.
- **Chemically**, it is highly reactive, forming a vast array of compounds, and serves as a powerful reducing agent.
- **Technologically**, hydrogen is a key player in clean‑energy strategies (fuel cells, hydrogen economy) and advanced research (fusion, MRI).

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
